sections.h2: Licking County housing and taxing districts
sections.html:
Licking County sits in central Ohio, with Newark as the county seat, and forms part of the Columbus metropolitan area. It had 185,564 residents in July 2025, up 4.0 percent from April 2020, and 73,930 housing units. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $275,200, homeownership reaches 73.7 percent, and half of households earn more than $84,426. Carrying costs average $1,693 a month with a loan and $631 free and clear, and tenants pay $1,078 in gross rent at the median.

A farm near Utica, a lot in Newark and a new build in New Albany fall into different school, township and city taxing districts, so equal values do not guarantee equal bills. New Albany alone adds more than 100 homes a year beside a nine-million-square-foot business park, which keeps pressure on land values at the county's western edge.

The county splits the job between two desks at 20 South Second Street in Newark. The auditor determines taxable values, certifies rates, administers the reduction programs and acts as secretary to the Board of Revision. The treasurer bills and collects real estate, manufactured home, estate and hotel and motel taxes plus special assessments.

  • Auditor: (740) 670-5040, weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:30 PM, closed on holidays.
  • Treasurer: 740-670-5010, on the same schedule.
  • Online lookup: both offices point to the county's OnTrac site for parcel search and tax information.
  • Deed work: the auditor stops same-day processing of conveyances, exempts, splits and merges at 4 p.m.

The 2026 Triennial Update of Licking County property values is complete, under Ohio Revised Code 5713.01. Owners can review the new values on OnTrac or at the auditor's counter during weekday office hours. Search your own parcel on OnTrac to see what changed, and compare the new value with what similar homes nearby recently sold for before deciding whether to file a complaint.

The state's schedule puts Licking mid-cycle in a six-year rotation: an update in 2026 and the next full reappraisal in 2029. Here are the dates and rules that matter most to an owner.

Licking County valuation and payment rules
Valuation or payment ruleWhat applies
Latest value update2026
Next full reappraisal2029
Value complaint filing dateMarch 31 after the tax year
Missed installmentTen percent added to the unpaid amount
Catch-up inside ten daysThat charge cut in half

Real estate tax comes in two installments. The exact deadlines print on each bill, and they can shift from one year to the next, so read the bill or phone 740-670-5010.

Section 323.121 sets the consequences. Missing an installment adds ten percent to what is unpaid, though a catch-up inside ten days cuts that charge in half. Interest on old balances starts the month after the second-half deadline and is posted again on December 1.

A mailed payment counts if the Postal Service postmark is dated on or before the last day. A postage-meter stamp from a private machine fails that test, under section 323.12.

sections.h2: How to contest a Licking County value
sections.html:
The auditor receives the complaint and hands it to the Board of Revision. Section 5715.19 sets the filing date at March 31 after the tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. A stamped postmark serves as the date of a mailed complaint.

  • The owner, the owner's spouse and certain professionals who hold a license and work for the owner can sign the filing.
  • A parcel gets one complaint per interim period. Exceptions cover an arm's length sale, damage from a casualty, a major improvement, or a 15 percent swing in occupancy.
  • The board sends notice of the hearing at least ten days ahead and has 180 days after the filing deadline to rule.
  • During the dispute the treasurer takes a payment based on the owner's claimed value.
  • Put every piece of evidence in front of the board, because material held back can be excluded on appeal.

Ask the auditor's office for the current complaint form and any filing instructions before you prepare the paperwork. Gather a recent sale price, an appraisal or photos of damage first, since a complaint with evidence attached is easier for the board to weigh.

sections.h2: What a seller meets at the auditor's counter
sections.html:
Before the recorder sees a deed, the auditor must. Section 319.202 has the grantee file a value statement and has the auditor mark the deed with the fee collected. The statement also covers any tax reduction or farm-use valuation that could pass to the buyer.

The grantor covers the state conveyance fee at this step. An added county levy exists only if commissioners enacted one under section 322.02, which limits it to 30 cents for every $100. Phone the auditor at (740) 670-5040 to learn whether Licking County has one. Farmland sellers should flag any past farm-use enrollment to the title company, because recoupment rides on the same filing.

Arrive before 4 p.m. if the transfer must clear that day.

sections.h2: Checking a parcel before you list
sections.html:
Both the auditor and the treasurer direct visitors to OnTrac, the county's online property site. It is the place for tax information and property search, and it is available around the clock, so a seller can check a parcel on a weekend before a closing.

Records of the deed itself live at the recorder's office in the same building, which accepts documents for recording between 8:30 AM and 4:15 PM on weekdays. Buyers' title companies pull the tax record and the recorded history together before setting a closing. A delinquent balance gets settled with the treasurer, whose office collects overdue real estate tax and assessments.

Special assessments sit with the treasurer as well. Ask which ones are open on the parcel so the closing figures include them.

Owing tax does not stop a sale, but it changes the order of events. Ask the treasurer for the amount due, including any ten percent charge, interest and open special assessments. Give that figure to your title company so it can be paid from the proceeds at closing. If you are close to a deadline, a catch-up payment inside ten days halves the ten percent charge, which can be cheaper than waiting for closing. Check also whether a value complaint is pending, since the treasurer takes payment based on your claimed value during a dispute and the final figure may change after the sale.

faqs.q: Which number reaches the right Licking County tax office?
faqs.a: Dial the treasurer at 740-670-5010 about payments and the auditor at (740) 670-5040 about values. Both sit at 20 South Second Street in Newark.

faqs.q: When is the next full reappraisal in Licking County?
faqs.a: The state schedule lists 2029 as the next reappraisal year for Licking County. The 2026 triennial update is already complete.

faqs.q: Can I contest my Licking County value every year?
faqs.a: No, the statute allows one complaint per parcel in each interim period. A second one needs a qualifying event: an arm's length sale, casualty damage, a substantial improvement, or a 15 percent occupancy change.

faqs.q: Is there a county transfer tax on a Licking County sale?
faqs.a: Ask the auditor, since the tax exists only where commissioners passed a resolution for it. The state conveyance fee is a separate charge that the seller pays at the auditor's counter.

faqs.q: What if I skip a Licking County installment?
faqs.a: Ten percent is added to the unpaid half, and a payment inside ten days earns a 50 percent reduction of that charge. Interest then builds on overdue balances, so call the treasurer early.
